claim: MCMV activates the IRE1-XBP1 pathway early post infection to relieve repression by XBP1u.
source: MCMV activates the IRE1-XBP1 pathway early post infection to relieve repression by XBP1u, the product of the unspliced Xbp1 mRNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by experimental data showing transient XBP1 splicing between 5-7 hours post infection (Figure 1A) and replication defects in IRE1-deficient cells.

claim: XBP1u inhibits viral gene expression and replication by blocking the activation of the viral major immediate-early promoter by XBP1s and ATF6.
source: XBP1u inhibits viral gene expression and replication by blocking the activation of the viral major immediate-early promoter by XBP1s and ATF6.
evidence: This claim is supported by luciferase reporter assays showing XBP1u represses MIEP activity (Figure 7E-G) and viral replication data showing impaired replication when unspliceable XBP1 is expressed (Figure 5D).

claim: XBP1s and ATF6 have redundant functions as activators of the viral life cycle.
source: These findings reveal a redundant function of XBP1s and ATF6 as activators of the viral life cycle, and an unexpected role of XBP1u as a potent repressor of both XBP1s and ATF6-mediated activation.
evidence: This is supported by data showing that loss of either XBP1 or ATF6 alone does not impair MCMV replication (Figures 3B, 6B), but loss of both substantially reduces replication (Figure 6D).

claim: MCMV infection causes a transient increase of XBP1 splicing between 5 and 7 hours post infection.
source: We detected a short and transient increase of XBP1 splicing between 5 and 7 hr post infection (hpi) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by qRT-PCR data quantifying spliced and unspliced XBP1 transcripts shown in Figure 1A.

claim: XBP1 splicing during MCMV infection is massively reduced when cells are infected with UV-inactivated MCMV.
source: This increase was massively reduced when cells were infected with UV-inactivated MCMV (Figure 1A), suggesting that XBP1 splicing was not caused by viral attachment and entry into cells but required viral gene expression.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing active and UV-inactivated MCMV shown in Figure 1A.

claim: XBP1 splicing during MCMV infection requires viral gene expression.
source: This increase was massively reduced when cells were infected with UV-inactivated MCMV (Figure 1A), suggesting that XBP1 splicing was not caused by viral attachment and entry into cells but required viral gene expression.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that UV-inactivated virus (which cannot express genes) does not induce XBP1 splicing.

claim: MCMV-induced XBP1 splicing is suppressed by cycloheximide.
source: MCMV-induced XBP1 splicing was suppressed by cycloheximide (CHX, a translation inhibitor), but not by phosphonoacetic acid (PAA), an inhibitor of viral DNA replication and late gene expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C comparing CHX and PAA treatment effects.

claim: MCMV-induced XBP1 splicing is not suppressed by phosphonoacetic acid.
source: MCMV-induced XBP1 splicing was suppressed by cycloheximide (CHX, a translation inhibitor), but not by phosphonoacetic acid (PAA), an inhibitor of viral DNA replication and late gene expression (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The transient activation of the IRE1-XBP1 pathway is caused by viral proteins expressed at immediate-early or early times post infection.
source: These results suggested that the transient activation of the IRE1-XBP1 pathway is caused by viral proteins expressed at immediate-early or early times post infection.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that CHX (which blocks translation) suppresses XBP1 splicing, while PAA (which blocks late gene expression) does not.

claim: IRE1 is necessary for efficient replication of MCMV.
source: Thus, we concluded that IRE1 is necessary for efficient replication of MCMV, but needs to be carefully regulated as too high expression levels are detrimental for cell viability and viral replication.
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data showing reduced MCMV titers in IRE1-deficient cells and cells with very low or very high IRE1 expression (Figures 2B, 2C).

claim: Too high IRE1 expression levels are detrimental for cell viability and viral replication.
source: Thus, we concluded that IRE1 is necessary for efficient replication of MCMV, but needs to be carefully regulated as too high expression levels are detrimental for cell viability and viral replication.
evidence: This is supported by cell viability data (Figure 2D) and replication kinetics showing reduced viral titers at high doxycycline concentrations (Figures 2B, 2C).

claim: IRE1 overexpression is cytotoxic.
source: This is consistent with the previously reported cytotoxicity of IRE1 overexpression (Han et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by Han et al., 2009.

claim: In Ern1 ko MEFs, viral replication and viral gene transcription were massively reduced compared to WT MEFs.
source: In Ern1 ko MEFs, viral replication (Figure 3B) and viral gene transcription (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) were massively reduced as compared to WT MEFs (Figure 3B)
evidence: This is directly supported by replication kinetics data (Figure 3B) and transcript quantification data (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).

claim: MCMV replication is virtually unimpaired in the absence of Xbp1.
source: By contrast, MCMV replication was virtually unimpaired in the absence of Xbp1 (Figure 3B) or Traf2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: MCMV replication is virtually unimpaired in the absence of Traf2.
source: By contrast, MCMV replication was virtually unimpaired in the absence of Xbp1 (Figure 3B) or Traf2 (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The expression of viral immediate-early, early, and late proteins is reduced in Ern1 ko MEFs compared to WT MEFs.
source: Compared to WT MEFs, the expression of all three proteins was reduced in Ern1 ko MEFs (Figure 3D), but not in Xbp1 or Traf2 ko MEFs (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The expression of viral immediate-early, early, and late proteins is not reduced in Xbp1 ko MEFs compared to WT MEFs.
source: Compared to WT MEFs, the expression of all three proteins was reduced in Ern1 ko MEFs (Figure 3D), but not in Xbp1 or Traf2 ko MEFs (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The expression of viral immediate-early, early, and late proteins is not reduced in Traf2 ko MEFs compared to WT MEFs.
source: Compared to WT MEFs, the expression of all three proteins was reduced in Ern1 ko MEFs (Figure 3D), but not in Xbp1 or Traf2 ko MEFs (Figure 3E and F).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The RNase activity of IRE1 is necessary for efficient MCMV replication.
source: While expression of WT IRE1 restored MCMV replication to high titers, expression of IRE1-K907A did not increase MCMV titers (Figure 4B), indicating that the IRE1 RNase activity is necessary for efficient MCMV replication.
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data comparing WT IRE1 and RNase-dead IRE1-K907A mutant (Figure 4B).

claim: MCMV replication is severely impaired upon expression of unspliceable Xbp1 transcript.
source: Whereas re-introduction of WT XBP1 had no detrimental effect, MCMV replication was severely impaired upon expression of the unspliceable Xbp1 transcript (Figure 5D), indicating that Xbp1u reduces viral replication.
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: XBP1u reduces viral replication.
source: Whereas re-introduction of WT XBP1 had no detrimental effect, MCMV replication was severely impaired upon expression of the unspliceable Xbp1 transcript (Figure 5D), indicating that Xbp1u reduces viral replication.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that expression of unspliceable XBP1 (which produces only XBP1u) impairs viral replication.

claim: A similar inhibitory effect on MCMV replication was observed when the truncated XBP1 protein was expressed.
source: A similar inhibitory effect was observed when the truncated XBP1 protein was expressed (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: MCMV replicated to similar titers in Xbp1 ko and Xbp1/Ern1 double-knockout cells.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, MCMV replicated to similar titers in Xbp1 ko and Xbp1/Ern1 double-knockout (dko) cells, indicating that the loss of IRE1 is not detrimental for MCMV replication when XBP1 is absent.
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The loss of IRE1 is not detrimental for MCMV replication when XBP1 is absent.
source: As shown in Figure 5B, MCMV replicated to similar titers in Xbp1 ko and Xbp1/Ern1 double-knockout (dko) cells, indicating that the loss of IRE1 is not detrimental for MCMV replication when XBP1 is absent.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that Xbp1 ko and Xbp1/Ern1 dko cells support similar levels of viral replication.

claim: MCMV gene expression and replication were not impaired in Atf6-/- MEFs.
source: First, we analyzed MEFs from Atf6-/- mice and found that MCMV gene expression and replication were not impaired (Figure 6A and B).
evidence: This is supported by immunoblot analysis (Figure 6A) and replication kinetics data (Figure 6B).

claim: MCMV replication was substantially reduced in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells.
source: When we knocked out Xbp1 in Atf6-/- cells by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing (Figure 6C), MCMV replication was substantially reduced in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells (Figure 6D), suggesting that ATF6 and XBP1s have overlapping or redundant functions and that at least one of them is necessary for efficient MCMV replication.
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: ATF6 and XBP1s have overlapping or redundant functions and at least one of them is necessary for efficient MCMV replication.
source: When we knocked out Xbp1 in Atf6-/- cells by CRISPR/Cas9 gene editing (Figure 6C), MCMV replication was substantially reduced in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells (Figure 6D), suggesting that ATF6 and XBP1s have overlapping or redundant functions and that at least one of them is necessary for efficient MCMV replication.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that loss of either factor alone does not impair replication, but loss of both does.

claim: The MCMV MIEP contains five ACGT motifs.
source: Five ACGT motifs were identified within the MCMV MIEP (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MIEP activity was strongly reduced in Ern1 ko cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, MIEP activity was strongly reduced in Ern1 ko cells but was not significantly altered in Xbp1 ko cells.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MIEP activity was not significantly altered in Xbp1 ko cells.
source: As shown in Figure 7B, MIEP activity was strongly reduced in Ern1 ko cells but was not significantly altered in Xbp1 ko cells.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: MIEP activity was not reduced in Xbp1/Ern1 dko cells compared to the parental Xbp1 ko cell.
source: MIEP activity was not reduced in Xbp1/Ern1 dko cells compared to the parental Xbp1 ko cell (Figure 7C), but was significantly reduced in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells compared to the parental Atf6-/- cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: MIEP activity was significantly reduced in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells compared to the parental Atf6-/- cells.
source: MIEP activity was not reduced in Xbp1/Ern1 dko cells compared to the parental Xbp1 ko cell (Figure 7C), but was significantly reduced in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells compared to the parental Atf6-/- cells (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Activation of the MCMV MIEP correlated with viral replication in the same cells.
source: Thus, we concluded that activation of the MCMV MIEP correlated with viral replication in the same cells.
evidence: This inference is based on comparing MIEP activity data (Figure 7) with viral replication data (Figures 5B and 6D).

claim: The activity of the MIEP had a substantially reduced activity when all 5 ACGT motifs were mutated.
source: We also found that the activity of the MIEP had a substantially reduced activity when all 5 ACGT motifs were mutated (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figures 7B-D.

claim: MIEP activity was slightly increased by expression of XBP1s in Xbp1 ko cells.
source: In Xbp1 ko cells, MIEP activity was slightly increased by expression of XBP1s, but substantially reduced by XBP1u.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: MIEP activity was substantially reduced by XBP1u in Xbp1 ko cells.
source: In Xbp1 ko cells, MIEP activity was slightly increased by expression of XBP1s, but substantially reduced by XBP1u.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: XBP1u antagonized XBP1s in a dose-dependent manner.
source: XBP1u also antagonized XBP1s in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: MIEP activity was slightly increased by expression of ATF6(N) in Atf6-/- cells.
source: A similar result was obtained in Atf6-/- cells: MIEP activity was slightly increased by expression of ATF6(N), but substantially reduced by XBP1u.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: MIEP activity was substantially reduced by XBP1u in Atf6-/- cells.
source: A similar result was obtained in Atf6-/- cells: MIEP activity was slightly increased by expression of ATF6(N), but substantially reduced by XBP1u.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: XBP1u antagonized ATF6(N) in a dose-dependent manner in Atf6-/- cells.
source: XBP1u also antagonized ATF6(N) in a dose-dependent manner (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Expression of either XBP1s or ATF6(N) was sufficient to increase MIEP activity substantially in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells.
source: In Atf6/Xbp1 dko cell, expression of either XBP1s or ATF6(N) was sufficient to increase MIEP activity substantially.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: XBP1u alone did not reduce MIEP activity in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells.
source: XBP1u alone did not reduce MIEP activity in these cells, but it antagonized the activity of ATF6(N) expressed by transfection (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: XBP1u antagonized the activity of ATF6(N) expressed by transfection in Atf6/Xbp1 dko cells.
source: XBP1u alone did not reduce MIEP activity in these cells, but it antagonized the activity of ATF6(N) expressed by transfection (Figure 7G).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 7G.

claim: Both XBP1s and ATF6(N) can activate the MCMV MIEP in a largely redundant fashion.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that both, XBP1s and ATF6(N), can activate the MCMV MIEP in a largely redundant fashion, and that XBP1u represses the activity of both, XBP1s and ATF6(N).
evidence: This inference is based on luciferase reporter assay data showing that either XBP1s or ATF6(N) can activate the MIEP (Figure 7).

claim: XBP1u represses the activity of both XBP1s and ATF6(N).
source: Taken together, these results suggest that both, XBP1s and ATF6(N), can activate the MCMV MIEP in a largely redundant fashion, and that XBP1u represses the activity of both, XBP1s and ATF6(N).
evidence: This inference is based on luciferase reporter assay data showing XBP1u antagonizes both XBP1s and ATF6(N) (Figures 7E-G).

claim: XBP1s and XBP1u showed the strongest interaction with motifs 3 and 4 in DPI-ELISA.
source: In this DPI-ELISA, XBP1s and XBP1u showed the strongest interaction with motifs 3 and 4, whereas ATF6(N) interacted with motifs 2 and 4 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by DPI-ELISA data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: ATF6(N) interacted with motifs 2 and 4 in DPI-ELISA.
source: In this DPI-ELISA, XBP1s and XBP1u showed the strongest interaction with motifs 3 and 4, whereas ATF6(N) interacted with motifs 2 and 4 (Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by DPI-ELISA data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: ACGT motif 4 is necessary for MIEP activation by XBP1s and ATF6(N).
source: As shown in Figure 9A, XBP1s or ATF6(N) expression increased the activity of all MIEP constructs except MIEP-4-mut and MIEP-all-mut, indicating that ACGT motif 4 is necessary for MIEP activation by XBP1s and ATF6(N).
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Motif 4 is sufficient to confer MIEP responsiveness to XBP1s and ATF6.
source: Indeed, MIEP-4-only was inducible by XBP1s and ATF6(N) (Figure 9B), suggesting that motif 4 is sufficient to confer MIEP responsiveness to XBP1s and ATF6.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data showing that a MIEP with only motif 4 intact can be activated by XBP1s and ATF6(N) (Figure 9B).

claim: Viral replication was massively reduced when motif 4 within the MIEP was mutated.
source: Indeed, viral replication was massively reduced when motif 4 within the MIEP was mutated.
evidence: This is supported by replication kinetics data comparing MCMV-GFP and MCMV-GFP-4-mut (Figure 9C).

claim: The XBP1 and ATF6(N) target motif identified in DNA-binding and luciferase reporter assays is required for efficient replication of the virus.
source: This result confirmed that the XBP1 and ATF6(N) target motif identified in DNA-binding and luciferase reporter assays is required for efficient replication of the virus.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that mutation of motif 4 reduces both MIEP activity in reporter assays and viral replication.

claim: MCMV transiently activates the IRE1-XBP1 signaling pathway in the early phase of infection in order to relieve XBP1u-mediated repression of viral gene expression and replication.
source: Taken together, the results of this study show that MCMV transiently activates the IRE1-XBP1 signaling pathway in the early phase of infection in order to relieve XBP1u-mediated repression of viral gene expression and replication.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on multiple experimental findings including XBP1 splicing kinetics, replication defects in IRE1-deficient cells, and XBP1u repression of MIEP activity.

claim: The MCMV major immediate-early promoter requires XBP1s or ATF6(N) binding to motif 4 for full activation.
source: The MCMV major immediate-early promoter requires XBP1s or ATF6(N) binding to motif 4 for full activation, and XBP1u prevents promoter activity by both TFs.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assays (Figures 7, 9) and DPI-ELISA data (Figure 8).

claim: XBP1u prevents MIEP promoter activity by both XBP1s and ATF6(N).
source: The MCMV major immediate-early promoter requires XBP1s or ATF6(N) binding to motif 4 for full activation, and XBP1u prevents promoter activity by both TFs.
evidence: This is supported by luciferase reporter assay data showing XBP1u represses MIEP activation by both XBP1s and ATF6(N) (Figures 7E-G).

claim: XBP1u acts as a key repressor of two UPR pathways, the IRE1-XBP1 and the ATF6 pathways, which have overlapping and redundant functions.
source: Thus, XBP1u acts as a key repressor of two UPR pathways, the IRE1-XBP1 and the ATF6 pathways, which have overlapping and redundant functions.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on data showing XBP1u represses both XBP1s and ATF6(N) activity, and that these two factors have redundant functions.

claim: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is a cellular homeostatic circuit regulating protein synthesis and processing in the ER by three ER-to-nucleus signaling pathways.
source: The unfolded protein response (UPR) is a cellular homeostatic circuit regulating protein synthesis and processing in the ER by three ER-to-nucleus signaling pathways.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the UPR.

claim: One UPR pathway is triggered by the inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1), which splices the X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1) mRNA, thereby enabling expression of XBP1s.
source: One pathway is triggered by the inositol-requiring enzyme 1 (IRE1), which splices the X-box binding protein 1 (Xbp1) mRNA, thereby enabling expression of XBP1s.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the IRE1-XBP1 pathway.

claim: Another UPR pathway activates the activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6).
source: Another UPR pathway activates the activating transcription factor 6 (ATF6).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the ATF6 pathway.

claim: When protein synthesis is increased or ER function is compromised, the folding capacity of the ER may get out of balance, leading to an accumulation of unfolded or misfolded proteins in the ER.
source: When protein synthesis is increased or ER function is compromised, the folding capacity of the ER may get out of balance, leading to an accumulation of unfolded or misfolded proteins in the ER.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ER stress.

claim: The UPR leads to a reduced protein synthesis and an increased expression of folding chaperones and ER-associated degradation (ERAD) factors.
source: To alleviate ER stress and restore homeostasis, the cell activates three ER-to-nucleus signaling pathways, collectively called the unfolded protein response (UPR), which lead to a reduced protein synthesis and an increased expression of folding chaperones and ER-associated degradation (ERAD) factors (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: In mammalian cells, the UPR comprises three main signaling pathways named after the initiating ER stress sensors: PERK, ATF6, and IRE1.
source: In mammalian cells, the UPR comprises three main signaling pathways named after the initiating ER stress sensors: PERK (PKR-like ER kinase), ATF6 (activating transcription factor 6), and IRE1 (inositol-requiring enzyme 1) (Walter and Ron, 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Walter and Ron, 2011.

claim: Upon activation by ER stress, PERK phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2α, which leads to a massive attenuation of protein synthesis.
source: Upon activation by ER stress, PERK phosphorylates the translation initiation factor eIF2α, which leads to a massive attenuation of protein synthesis and an immediate reduction of the protein load in the secretory system.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about the PERK pathway.

claim: Phosphorylated eIF2α selectively supports the translation of selected cellular proteins such as the transcription factor ATF4.
source: However, phosphorylated eIF2α selectively supports the translation of selected cellular proteins such as the transcription factor ATF4, which activates a negative feedback loop resulting in dephosphorylation of eIF2α (Novoa et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Novoa et al., 2001.

claim: Upon activation by ER stress, ATF6 travels to the Golgi, where it undergoes intramembrane proteolysis.
source: Upon activation by ER stress, ATF6 travels to the Golgi, where it undergoes intramembrane proteolysis.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ATF6 processing.

claim: Intramembrane proteolysis of ATF6 liberates its cytosolic N-terminus, the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factor ATF6(N), and enables it to travel to the nucleus.
source: This process liberates its cytosolic N-terminus, the basic leucine zipper (bZIP) transcription factor ATF6(N), and enables it to travel to the nucleus, where it activates the transcription of chaperone genes as well as of the gene encoding XBP1 (Lee et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Lee et al., 2002.

claim: IRE1 is an ER transmembrane protein kinase that oligomerizes upon accumulation of unfolded proteins in the ER lumen.
source: The third sensor, IRE1 (also known as ER-to-nucleus signaling 1, ERN1), is an ER transmembrane protein kinase that oligomerizes upon accumulation of unfolded proteins in the ER lumen.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about IRE1 activation.

claim: Oligomerization and auto-transphosphorylation activate the RNase function of IRE1, which mediates an unconventional splicing of the XBP1 mRNA in the cytosol.
source: Oligomerization and auto-transphosphorylation activate the RNase function of IRE1, which mediates an unconventional splicing of the XBP1 mRNA in the cytosol (Calfon et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2001).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Calfon et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2002; Yoshida et al., 2001.

claim: Removal of the 26-nt intron from the XBP1 mRNA leads to a frame shift and expression of transcription factor XBP1s.
source: Removal of the 26-nt intron from the XBP1 mRNA leads to a frame shift and expression of transcription factor XBP1s, comprising an N-terminal basic leucine zipper (bZIP) domain followed by a C-terminal transcription activation domain.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about XBP1 mRNA splicing.

claim: The unspliced XBP1 mRNA encodes XBP1u, which lacks the transcription activation domain but contains in its C-terminal part a hydrophobic patch and a translational pausing region.
source: By contrast, the unspliced XBP1 mRNA encodes XBP1u, which lacks the transcription activation domain but contains in its C-terminal part a hydrophobic patch and a translational pausing region required for the recruitment of its own mRNA to the ER membrane (Kanda et al., 2016; Yanagitani et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Kanda et al., 2016; Yanagitani et al., 2011.

claim: XBP1u is rapidly degraded and has a short half-life.
source: XBP1u is rapidly degraded and has a short half-life (Tirosh et al., 2006).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Tirosh et al., 2006.

claim: XBP1u can interact with XBP1s and ATF6(N) and target them for proteasomal degradation.
source: It can interact with XBP1s and ATF6(N) and target them for proteasomal degradation. Therefore, XBP1u is thought to act as a negative regulator involved in fine-tuning the UPR (Tirosh et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Tirosh et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2009.

claim: XBP1u is thought to act as a negative regulator involved in fine-tuning the UPR.
source: Therefore, XBP1u is thought to act as a negative regulator involved in fine-tuning the UPR (Tirosh et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Tirosh et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2006; Yoshida et al., 2009.

claim: XBP1u affects autophagy by interacting with transcription factor FOXO1.
source: Moreover, XBP1u affects autophagy by interacting with transcription factor FOXO1 (Zhao et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2013.

claim: IRE1 can cleave ER-associated mRNA molecules that contain a specific recognition motif through a process called regulated IRE1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD).
source: Apart from mediating XBP1 mRNA splicing, IRE1 can also cleave ER-associated mRNA molecules that contain a specific recognition motif (Moore and Hollien, 2015). This process, which leads to mRNA degradation, is called regulated IRE1-dependent mRNA decay (RIDD).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Moore and Hollien, 2015.

claim: The importance of RIDD in different cellular processes such as lipid metabolism, antigen presentation, and apoptosis remains incompletely understood.
source: However, the importance of RIDD in different cellular processes such as lipid metabolism, antigen presentation, and apoptosis remains incompletely understood (Maurel et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge supported by citation to Maurel et al., 2014.

claim: During viral replication large quantities of viral proteins must be synthesized.
source: During viral replication large quantities of viral proteins must be synthesized.
evidence: This is general scientific knowledge about viral replication.

claim: Folding, maturation, and posttranslational modification of secreted and transmembrane proteins take place in the ER.
source: Folding, maturation, and posttranslational modification of secreted and transmembrane proteins take place in the ER and require a plethora of chaperones, foldases, and glycosylating enzymes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about ER function.

claim: Properly folded proteins are transported to the Golgi, while unfolded or misfolded proteins are retained in the ER and exported to the cytosol for proteasomal degradation via the ERAD pathway.
source: While properly folded proteins are transported to the Golgi, unfolded or misfolded proteins are retained in the ER and exported to the cytosol for proteasomal degradation via the ERAD pathway (Smith et al., 2011).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Smith et al., 2011.

claim: High levels of viral envelope glycoproteins synthesized during the late phase of the viral life cycle can overwhelm the folding and processing capacity of the ER.
source: However, the high levels of viral envelope glycoproteins that are being synthesized particularly during the late phase of the viral life cycle can overwhelm the folding and processing capacity of the ER and cause accumulation of unfolded and misfolded proteins in the ER (Zhang and Wang, 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citation to Zhang and Wang, 2012.

claim: Cytomegaloviruses (CMVs) are prototypic members of the β subfamily of the Herpesviridae.
source: Cytomegaloviruses (CMVs) are prototypic members of the β subfamily of the Herpesviridae.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about CMV classification.

claim: CMV genomes contain at least 165 protein-coding ORFs.
source: Their large double-stranded DNA genomes contain at least 165 protein-coding ORFs (Dolan et al., 2004) end encode an even larger number of polypeptides (Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Dolan et al., 2004 and Stern-Ginossar et al., 2012.

claim: CMVs have acquired the ability to moderate immune recognition and modulate cellular stress responses through millions of years of co-evolution with their hosts.
source: Through millions of years of co-evolution with their respective hosts, the CMVs have acquired the ability to moderate immune recognition and modulate cellular stress responses to their own benefit (Alwine, 2008; Mocarski, 2002).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Alwine, 2008 and Mocarski, 2002.

claim: HCMV and MCMV induce PERK activation, but limit eIF2α phosphorylation.
source: For instance, human and murine CMV (HCMV and MCMV) induce PERK activation, but limit eIF2α phosphorylation. By doing this the CMVs prevent a global protein synthesis shutoff but allow eIF2α phosphorylation-dependent activation of transcription factor ATF4 (Isler et al., 2005; Qian et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge supported by citations to Isler et al., 2005 and Qian et al., 2012.

claim: CMVs increase expression of the ER chaperone BiP to facilitate protein folding and virion assembly.

source: Moreover, a truncated XBP1 protein, XBP1stop, which lacks the C-terminal destabilizing domain of XBP1u, had a similar repressive effect as XBP1u (Figure 5D) indicating that destabilization is not required for repression.
evidence: This inference is based on the observation that XBP1stop, which lacks the destabilizing domain, still represses viral replication.

source: The results of our study show that XBP1u plays a very important role as a repressor of XBP1s and ATF6(N)-mediated activation of the MCMV MIEP, which results in a massively (up to 100-fold) reduced production of progeny virus (Figures 2, 3B and 5D).

claim: In IRE1-deficient cells, the Xbp1 transcript is expressed from its endogenous promoter, not from a strong heterologous promoter.

evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design used in the study.

claim: The observed effects of XBP1u cannot be dismissed as overexpression artifacts.

evidence: This inference is based on the experimental design where XBP1u is expressed from the endogenous promoter.

In light of our data showing a redundancy of XBP1s and ATF6(N) in the activation of the MCMV MIEP, this conjecture may well be correct.
